per_item.reference: All three, then, and each one alone would have stalled it. The watering third: each layer is watered as it is laid, because water poured over a finished heap runs off the outside and leaves the middle dry, which is exactly what you found. draws.answer: Then two things are missing. The catalogue says to chop up the plant residues that rot fast, and that fast rotting residues are straw and groundnut, soy and cowpea leaves. Chopped stalks of sorghum, millet or maize are among those, along with the leaves of groundnut, soy and cowpea. And on top of it, the watering: it says you must water each layer as you lay it, not simply after the heap is laid. Three things to put in the heap, in order. The slow rotting material, chopped: rice husks and ronier leaves. And a little wood ash on the topsoil. And water each layer as you lay it.

Then two of its four steps are right. The stalks and the husks are the two that rot fast, so they are where it rotts first, which is the instruction to chop them up quickly and in a heap. The order is the order of working, so the other three are not wrong in the way of the heap: the site, which should be a shaded spot, easy to reach, with water nearby; the layers, watered as you lay them, one layer at a time, so that every layer has a place; the activator, which is rice husks or ronier leaves trodden down first, then topsoil or well rotted compost spread lightly; then topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri among the activator. The last is the one with the instruction you will want most: a manure pit well away from the heap, because rain watered is spread over it and it evaporates at the end. And the watering once a heap is finished is not enough of it, since the catalogue says to keep it damp, not to water it.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference works on 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders, 50 for chicks and 12 to 15 for the growers, and the 2017 ESFT village compendium works on 5 to 6 hens per square metre for the improved family henhouse, so I also need to know which of the two you are building.
Seven metres by four, the commercial model, and I want breeders and growers both.

draws.answer: Then you are building the commercial model, which is 14 square metres at 8 to 10 birds per square metre, so 112 birds at 14 per square metre, with room left for two or three years of stock. That is the compartment the commercial reference asks for, because it gives its own sizes for the improved family henhouse: at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, one with a shared yard for the breeders and one for the brooding cocks, and tarpaulins kept to close against rain and wind. The 2017 village compendium works on a different layout for that, with breeders at 4 m by 3.5 m and growers at 5 by 2, so three times four and two times three, 42 by 14. Tell me which of the two you are building, since they are not interchangeable.

Then you are near the minimum, and the 2017 compendium's own figures for that mix are 60 hens and 6 cocks, at one cock for ten hens, and they are for the improved family henhouse of the 2020 reference, which is the model for the housing of the better hens rather than the bigger commercial nucleus, so the building is smaller than your numbers. Two things to know about it and about the other size. The improved family henhouse of 2020 is built for 60 hens and 6 cocks, so the building you are building is within reach, but it is not the same: the 2017 compendium says to plan the densities for the age, the chicks being under three months, at 8 to 10 per square metre. And the 2019 village compendium's reference, which is the one closest to your building, says the commercial model works on 8 to 10 breeding hens per square metre and 50 to 60 growers per square metre. So two things to check before you build: check if your flock is at the level the model is built for, and check whether you can fill it.

per_item.reference: No. More urea than recommended does not give more maize: over-dosing wastes your money and can even cut the yield. For maize, the ITRA and ICAT fiche gives about 100 kg of urea per hectare, put at panicle initiation, 30 to 45 days after sowing, in a pocket away from the stem so it does not burn the plant. What raises the harvest is putting the right amount at the right time, after the base NPK, and keeping the weeding on schedule. If you think your soil needs more, ask ICAT for an adjustment to your soil.

per_item.reference: No, the cycles overlap. A bird takes twenty-one days of incubation and then six months to reach sale weight, about 1.3 kg for a hen and 1.5 kg for a cock, so no bird goes from egg to sale in two months. Six production cycles a year in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference means six settings running at different stages at the same time: one batch in the incubator or under hens, one in the brooder for its first three weeks, one in the chick room, others in the grower compartments for the 3 to 6 month birds. That is also why the reference asks for at least five compartments: several ages are on the farm at once by design.

history.content: Six cycles a year means a bird goes from egg to sale in two months.

draws.answer: Six cycles a year means six batches a year, and six batches a year is six sales a year. So the two things are tied, not one telling the other. The six batches is what the model is for: six production cycles a year, with six units sold, and it is the same product, six birds per bird over the year. Your six sales are a year of six batches, two of which may not be sold, which is what makes the net result per bird a little below the unit. The two figures come from the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, which is the same study that sets out the commercial model for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks.

Six cycles a year means about six batches a year, not two. The six production cycles are the six production cycles per year of 120 eggs laid per hen per laying over the three years, not the two you want sold each year. What you are sold is eggs, which you can keep for two or three years, and you sell them after hatching at six months or more, at 24 months for hens. That is the opposite order: keeping them six months while selling them two or three months.

per_item.reference: Look under the leaves of your tomato plants every week to detect any tiny insects. Turn each leaf over and count the insects on a few plants before you decide on any spray. If the insects are numerous, prune the most infested leaves and destroy them. Remove weeds from the plot edges that can serve as a refuge for the pests. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and a strong water jet to wash off aphids, while ladybirds and lacewings will naturally suppress them. For the approved product and dosage, contact ICAT.

history.content: The leaves on my tomatoes are yellowing and I hear a faint buzzing, what's the first thing I should do?

draws.answer: First, shake the plant and look at the underside of the leaves to see which pest is present, because whiteflies and aphids need different treatments. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on several plants before you decide to spray. If whiteflies are many, use yellow sticky traps to catch the adults. If aphids are many, use a strong jet of water on the leaves and encourage ladybirds and lacewings that naturally control them. Remove and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

The symptoms you describe are tomato sucking pests, so first shake the plant and look at the underside of the leaves to identify which pest you have, because each needs a different treatment. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants before choosing to spray. If many insects are found, pick off the most infested leaves and destroy them, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that can host the pests. For whiteflies, use yellow sticky traps; for aphids, spray a strong jet of water and rely on ladybirds and lacewings. If the infestation is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

per_item.reference: From the Ministry and PASA catalogue of good practices. Year one, improving plants, the legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen: beans, groundnut, cowpea. Year two, a hungry plant that consumes a lot, maize, the soil now being rich in nitrogen. Year three, a root or tuber crop that goes for the nutrients left deeper, yam. Year four, an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then back to year one with legumes. Before fixing it, take account of your soil's fertility and of last season's crop.

history.content: rotation 4 ans exemple

draws.answer: Year one, improving plants: legumes such as groundnut, cowpea or soya. Year two, a hungry plant that simply needs more of what it takes: maize. Year three, a root or tuber crop such as yam. Year four, an undemanding plant like okra. Then back to year one. The maize is the one that uses the most of the three, which is why the maize is always the first year crop.

Year one: beans, the improving plant that consumes a lot of nitrogen. Year two: maize, the hungry plant that takes a little nitrogen, sown when the rains are established, at 20 to 25 cm per seed. Year three: a root or tuber crop that goes down for the nutrients left deeper, such as yam. Year four: a tolerant variety of maize, the one the brochure says reduces the variety that needed weeding. Then back to year one. That is the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure's own example of a rotation.

per_item.reference: Transplant seedlings after about 21 days in the nursery, placing 2 to 3 plants per pocket spaced 20 by 20 centimetres. For lowland or irrigated fields, apply 200 kilograms per hectare of NPK 15-15-15 about a week after transplanting, then split 100 kilograms per hectare of urea, giving half at tillering and half at panicle initiation. Weed the field at 15 to 25 days after transplanting and again around 40 days. Protect the crop from birds from flowering until harvest. If you need variety matching or rate adjustments, see ICAT.

history.content: How should I transplant and fertilise my rice seedlings?

draws.answer: Transplant the rice seedlings after about 21 days in the nursery, putting two to three plants per pocket spaced 20 by 20 centimetres. Then, at 3-brain levels, distribute 200 kilograms of NPK 15-15-15 over your 10,000 m² field, which is 50 kilograms per hectare. Weed the field first at 15-25 days after transplant and again at about 40 days. Guard the crop against birds from flowering until harvest. For variety matching and fertilizer rates, see ICAT.

Transplant your rice seedlings at 20 by 20 centimetre spacing, placing two grains per pocket. About seven days after transplant, spread 200 kilograms per hectare of NPK 15-15-15 on each pocket. Then, at harvest, apply 100 kilograms per hectare of urea, which is the total recommended rate. Weed the field first at 15 to 25 days after transplanting and again at about 40 days. Keep birds away from the rice canopy from flowering until you harvest. For variety matching and rate adjustments, visit ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is not a pest problem; the maize is experiencing nitrogen depletion on a soil that has lost organic matter. First, look at the leaves: uniform pale yellow on the older lower leaves indicates nitrogen hunger. Second, avoid buying a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide based on a merchant's word, because mineral fertilizer alone often does not give a return on exhausted soil. Third, restore organic matter by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the proper dose for your plot. ICAT is the service to see.

history.content: My old maize field in Kara shows pale yellow older leavees while the new ones stay green, is it a pest?

draws.answer: That pattern is a sign of nitrogen shortage in the soil. First read the leaves; the uniform pale yellow on the old lower leaves means the plant is hungry for nitrogen, not a disease. Do not purchase a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide because mineral fertilizer alone often does not give a return on depleted soil. Bring the organic matter back by spreading manure, adding compost, or burying residues instead of burning them. Include a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your plot.

It is nitrogen loss in your maize field. Begin by opening a shallow drainage channel so water can run off the plot instead of staying. When the soil has drained, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg per hectare at panicle initiation and keep the fertilizer off the plant so it does not burn. Then continue with the second weeding and earthing-up as scheduled. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, go to ICAT for help.

per_item.reference: Then the count against the floor may be fine and the compartment still wrong. Check the number first: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on 8 to 10 breeders per square metre, 12 to 15 growers and 50 chicks, so measure and divide before anything else. If you are inside the figure, look at why one end is unused. The reference wants the henhouse well aired and roomy, with a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most, and tarpaulins kept to close against rain and wind, so a cold or wet end will empty. Check the feeders and drinkers are spread rather than grouped: for adults, one feeder of 150 cm by 12 by 16 for 25 birds, and four drinkers of 10 litres per hundred layers. And keep the compartments to their ages, since that is what the five compartment plan is for.

history.content: The birds are crowded at one end and the other end stays empty.

draws.answer: Then the second end is the problem, not the first: the reference asks for an improved commercial poultry house, and it names three things about the building that matter most at that moment, which are the chick room, the grower compartments and the drinkers, so the building is a starting point rather than a solution. The compartmented layouts are the one where the reference gives you the plan, with at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, one for the breeders at 8 to 10 birds per square metre, one for brooding at 12 to 15, two for chicks at 50 per square metre. Keep the feeders and drinkers to the rule that birds should have free choice of feed and water, and count the siphon drinkers per hundred birds as part of the stocking.

That is the end you are looking at, and it is the end that matters for the rules. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for an improved rooster from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, with a well developed bright red comb, on a nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks for a commercial unit. It also asks you to choose the cock from among your flock rather than buying him, because the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. So look for the one with the bright red comb. And clean around him, since the same reference says to keep the surroundings of the henhouse tidy, because a tuft of grass shelters the predators and the animals that bring disease.

When the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, and keep the fertilizer off the plant to avoid burn. Continue with the second weeding and earthing-up as scheduled. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, you should see ICAT.

history.content: After a heavy shower my corn's lower leaves are pale, especially where water pooled. Should I remove the plants?

draws.answer: The pale colour of the lower maize leaves after a heavy shower indicates nitrogen loss, not a disease. Open a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of standing. When the soil has drained, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, keeping the fertilizer off the plant so it does not burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you see any streaks on the veins or dead-heart symptoms, go to ICAT for help.

The pale lower leaves of your maize after a heavy rain are a sign of nitrogen loss, so you should not remove the plants. Do not purchase a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide because they will not correct the nitrogen deficiency. First, make a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of standing. When the soil has drained, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, using about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation and keep the fertilizer off the plant so it does not burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on their usual schedules. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, go to ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is bloat affecting your nanny goat. Immediately get the goat on its feet and keep it moving, holding its head raised to help belching. After that, drench a little vegetable or mineral oil into its mouth to break the froth and free the gas. This helps the rumen work again and lets the gas escape. The condition can lead to collapse very quickly. Call the veterinary service immediately for emergency assistance.

history.content: My nanny goat's left flank is tight, she stopped grazing and looks like she is struggling to breathe.

draws.answer: It is bloat in your nanny goat. Get her up and moving while keeping her head raised so she can try to belch the gas. Then drench a little vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the frothy foam in the rumen. Call the veterinary service right away because a severe case needs their intervention without delay. The veterinary service is the proper contact for this emergency.

Your nanny goat is experiencing bloat and needs urgent care. First, get the goat up and moving while keeping its head raised so it can belch the trapped gas. Then drench a little vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the froth and release the gas. After these actions, call the veterinary service immediately because a severe case needs their help without delay. The veterinary service is the appropriate service to call in this emergency.

per_item.reference: Your cattle have gall sickness (anaplasmosis). Call the veterinary service the same day because only they can confirm the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet that the urine is yellow-brown without red, which points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade, give it clean water within reach, and do not make it walk because it lacks red blood cells. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on the whole herd, not just the sick animal, to stop further spread. See the veterinary service the same day.

history.content: My cows are looking weak, they have yellow urine and seem to lag behind the herd.
Are the gums and eyelids pale or white?
Yes, their gums and eyelids are pale.

draws.answer: Your cattle have gall sickness, a tick-borne disease transmitted by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can identify the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine, which helps differentiate gall sickness from redwater. Keep the animal in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all ticks you see on the whole herd. Never use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service will provide the proper treatment.

Your cattle have redwater disease caused by Babesia. Call the veterinary service the same day and tell them the urine is red to black. They will identify the parasite and give the correct drug and dose. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not only on the sick animal. Never use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service is the only one you should see for diagnosis and treatment.

per_item.reference: Waiting with a small bag of beans after the harvest can be profitable. First, make sure the beans are stored well dried to keep them in good condition. Then keep that bag instead of selling the whole harvest immediately. When the lean season arrives, roughly June through August, prices usually go up. Check the weekly market day for your village and follow SIM cereal price updates on the radio before you decide to sell. Compare the local price plus transport cost with the price you might achieve in Lomé or other large markets. If you can, join a cooperative or sell together to reach larger buyers and cut per-bag transport cost. For more assistance, approach a cooperative or ICAT, and also ANSAT for grain.

history.content: I have a small bag of beans left after harvest. Is it smart to wait before selling?

draws.answer: The brochure does not say, and it is a simple fact of the country: be careful what you do with the beans after the harvest, because the small ones are what the study is built on, and it says to look for a good seller rather than at the first price. I will not invent a reason for it, because the catalogue gives none and a wrong one would send you to a seller who will sell at the lowest price. What it gives is the store and the market, so you are already in front of it. Ask ICAT or the cooperative, and ask the market day by day.

Waiting before you sell gives you time to find buyers and raises what you can charge. First, store the beans well dried. Then keep three to five tonnes past the harvest glut and look for your buyers before the first one comes up. Join or support a farmer's collective to reach bigger buyers and lower per-bag transport cost. Learn your area's cereal prices on the radio before you sell. If you cannot find buyers, consider drying and selling as a group or through a cooperative. For help, see a cooperative or ICAT, and ANSAT for grain.
